paper_metadata.title: A non-Schmid crystal plasticity finite element approach to multi-scale modeling of nickel-based superalloys

evidence.section: Abstract
evidence.quote: This paper develops non-Schmid crystal plasticity constitutive models at two length scales, and bridges them in a multi-scale framework. The constitutive models address thermo-mechanical behavior of Nickel-based superalloys for a large temperature range, viz. 300 K e1223 K, and include orientation dependencies and tension-compression asymmetry.

evidence.section: 3. Grain-scale crystal plasticity framework
evidence.quote: The homogenized single crystal grain-scale for FCC Nickel su-peralloys is obtained from parametrized representation of the morphology of the precipitates

evidence.section: 2.3 Calibration of parameters in the constitutive law
evidence.quote: The rest of the material constants in the constitutive model are calibrated from experiments on single crystal CMSX-4 in Ref. [11]. The alloy contains 70% volume fraction of predominantly cuboidal g0 precipitates of average size 0.45 mm.

evidence.section: 4.3. Validation of the homogenized single crystal grain-scale model
evidence.quote: experiments for single crystal of CMSX-4 with vp ¼ 70% of volume fraction of in the shape of cube as g’ precipitates ( n/∞). The average length of this cube is 0.45 mm and the average distance between precipitates is 0.05 mm which results in channel width lc ¼ 0.0866 mm.

evidence.section: 1. Introduction
evidence.quote: These alloys contain multiple phases including regular FCC crystal structure mainly Ni in g channel and L12 ordered crystal structure in g’ precipitates as indicated in Fig. 1.

evidence.section: 2.3 Calibration of parameters in the constitutive law
evidence.quote: The alloy contains 70% volume fraction of predominantly cuboidal g0 precipitates of average size 0.45 mm.

evidence.section: 2. Two-pahse g-g’ sub-grain scale of nickel superalloys
evidence.quote: The material studied is a two-phase, binary Nickel-based superalloy consisting of g(Ni) and g’(Ni3 Al) phases.

evidence.quote: As temperature increases dislocations in intermetallic g’ phase, which are mostly screw dislocations, tend to be locked in a Kear-Wilsdorf (KW) conﬁguration due to cross-slip [9].
